tagline: Prairie, desert and a mountain climb on the road to Alcova
intro: The Seminoe-Alcova Back Country Byway crosses prairie and desert before climbing the Seminoe Mountains in south central Wyoming. Its 64 miles combine pavement and gravel between Sinclair and Alcova; Wyoming’s tourism office gives a leisurely driving time of around two hours. The Bureau of Land Management presents the back country byway as a journey through changing landscapes, with three reservoirs and the Seminoe and Pedro mountains among its attractions.

An earlier journey here served the mines: in 1871, a freight and passenger line began linking them with the railroad, paralleling part of the present backway. Later, construction of Seminoe Dam and improvements to the road brought anglers and boaters into the area. Seminoe Dam was proposed as part of the Kendrick Project to regulate the North Platte and improve agriculture near Casper. Water storage began in 1939, followed that August by the project’s entry into operation.

Driving north, begin at Sinclair and follow County Road 351 toward the mountains. Beyond Seminoe State Park, the road becomes very steep through the Seminoe Mountains to the Miracle Mile. The byway crosses this stretch of the North Platte River before ending at Alcova. At the northern end, County Road 407 meets Wyoming Highway 220.

moments.title: Sinclair
moments.text: Sinclair began as Parco, a company town named for the Producers & Refiners Corporation, which founded both the town and its refinery. Built in 1924–1925, the planned community received a Spanish Colonial Revival design from Denver architects Fisher & Fisher. Its historic district includes a central plaza, worker housing, a theatre and a community church. The refinery just east of town remains in use, while the historic center became the Parco Historic District in 1987. The district’s name preserves Parco, the town’s original identity. The town was renamed after Sinclair Consolidated Oil Corporation acquired PARCO during the Great Depression.

moments.title: Seminoe Mountains
moments.text: The road’s steep climb north of Seminoe State Park carries it through a range that forms part of Seminoe Reservoir’s northern boundary. These mountains contain rocks dating back 2.7 billion years, and Bradley Peak is their primary landmark. Gold prospecting and iron ore discoveries followed in the late 1800s. The name comes from Basil Cimineau Lajeunesse, a French trapper and explorer active in the region during the nineteenth century. Seminoe is an Americanized spelling of Cimineau. At the base of the mountains, Seminoe State Park provides camping, boating and fishing facilities beside the reservoir.

moments.title: Miracle Mile
moments.text: The Miracle Mile extends five and a half river miles from the base of Kortes Dam downstream to Pathfinder Reservoir. The byway crosses this stretch of the North Platte, which the Bureau of Land Management identifies as a blue-ribbon trout fishery. Upstream, Kortes Dam impounds the river for hydroelectric power; the Bureau of Reclamation constructed the concrete gravity dam between 1946 and 1951.

practical: Seminoe Mountains: The byway is generally passable May to November. The steep section north of Seminoe State Park to the Miracle Mile is not recommended for motor homes or vehicles pulling trailers. There are no services until Alcova. (checked 2026-10-11)
